strengths: The main contribution is a useful, architecture-compatible optimization of RAFT-style correlation sampling. Patch-major storage, selectively computed correlation blocks, and caching across iterations exploit spatial and temporal locality without requiring model retraining or intentionally approximating the correlation operator.

The end-to-end benefits are substantial at the targeted resolutions. Table 3 reports 8K RAFT runtime decreasing from 11.00 to 4.59 seconds with nearly unchanged peak memory, and SEA-RAFT decreasing from 2.61 to 1.90 seconds. These demonstrate practical value beyond isolated kernel benchmarks.

The efficiency evaluation is extensive: it includes multiple optical-flow architectures, four GPU models, variations in resolution, feature dimensionality and iteration count, and a component breakdown. The caching ablation supports the design, reducing isolated runtime from 168.3 to 124.2 ms at 4096-pixel width.

The 8K benchmark provides a useful evaluation setting for fine details and large displacements. The simple cascaded SEA-RAFT extension requires no retraining and substantially improves native-resolution results: overall EPE falls from 17.63 to 2.70 and large-motion EPE from 107.39 to 21.56.

The supported systems contribution favors acceptance despite reservations about theoretical precision and claim scope. The supplement provides useful implementation details, benchmark configurations, scene identifiers, and a rendering script.
weaknesses: The stated O(P^1.5) space complexity does not describe the fixed-block implementation used in most experiments. Section 8.3 obtains this bound by choosing B = P^(1/8), whereas experiments generally fix B = 8, leaving the dense block mask with quadratic storage P^2/B^4. The analysis also needs to account explicitly for the number of cached iterations. This limits the claimed asymptotic scalability, although it does not negate the measured savings.

Exact operator equivalence is insufficiently documented. Algorithm 1 marks offsets only through r but subsequently gathers through r+1 for bilinear interpolation; near block boundaries, the extra interpolation neighbor can require an unmarked block. The block lookup also contains an unexplained additional subtraction of r. Reported unit tests and a 0.03% EPE difference are encouraging, but per-operator numerical comparisons and explicit boundary handling are needed to resolve these pseudocode inconsistencies.

The runtime and memory trade-off is less uniformly favorable than the prose suggests. At 8K, CCMR uses 66.68 GiB versus 36.30 GiB for on-demand sampling; at 4K, MS-RAFT+ uses 53.92 versus 24.22 GiB. Table 6 also shows the proposed sampler taking approximately twice the dense implementation's runtime at several smaller resolutions. Claims of similar memory to on-demand sampling and comparable dense-sampling runtime should be qualified.

The broad state-of-the-art accuracy claim is metric- and scale-dependent. Cascaded SEA-RAFT achieves the best reported overall and large-motion 1-pixel outlier rates, but its 8K EPE of 2.70 is worse than several lower-resolution alternatives. Table 7 reports MS-RAFT+ EPE of 1.63 at quarter resolution, versus 1.86 for cascaded SEA-RAFT. Table 2's emphasis on each competitor's highest feasible resolution obscures these operating points.

The UHR accuracy evidence comes from only three sequences of one synthetic movie; billions of evaluated pixels do not provide equivalent scene diversity. There is no per-sequence analysis or ablation of the cascade's threshold and scale factor, and applying the same initialization to other compatible methods would help establish whether the accuracy gain is specific to SEA-RAFT. These limitations primarily constrain the secondary accuracy contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical computer-vision bottleneck with a useful, architecture-compatible contribution. Patch-major organization, selectively computed correlation blocks, and caching exploit spatial and temporal locality without requiring model retraining. The contribution has value independently of benchmark-leading accuracy.

The end-to-end speedups are substantial at the target resolutions. Table 3 reports RAFT runtime decreasing from 11.00 to 4.59 seconds at 8K, and SEA-RAFT from 2.61 to 1.90 seconds. These comparisons use the feasible on-demand implementation rather than an infeasible dense baseline.

The evaluation extends well beyond a single favorable experiment: it includes multiple optical-flow architectures, four GPU models, resolution and feature-dimension sweeps, iteration counts, component timing, and a caching ablation. Supplementary results on Spring, Sintel, and KITTI further support practical applicability.

The 8K benchmark and cascaded inference provide useful supplementary contributions. Cascading reduces SEA-RAFT's native-resolution large-motion EPE from 107.39 to 21.56 and its overall 1-pixel outlier rate from 17.5% to 13.3%. Overall, the demonstrated efficiency contribution favors acceptance despite the qualifications below.
weaknesses: The advertised O(P^1.5) memory complexity does not describe the evaluated fixed-block implementation. Section 8.3 obtains this bound by choosing B = P^(1/8), whereas experiments use B = 8 or 16. With fixed B, the explicitly stored computation mask has (P/B^2)^2 entries and therefore remains asymptotically quadratic. The analysis also needs to state its fixed-iteration assumption when accounting for cached blocks. This limits the theoretical claim, although it does not negate the measured memory savings.

Exact operator equivalence is insufficiently documented. Algorithm 1 marks offsets through r but subsequently gathers through r+1 for bilinear interpolation; as written, this can request an unmarked neighboring block. Its block lookup also contains an unexplained additional subtraction of r. These may be pseudocode errors rather than implementation failures, but the reported 0.03% downstream EPE difference and unspecified unit tests do not resolve them. Direct numerical comparisons covering block boundaries, padding, and out-of-bounds queries would substantiate the central exactness claim.

The memory/runtime trade-off is less uniformly favorable than the prose suggests. In Table 3, MS-RAFT+ at half resolution uses 53.92 GiB versus 24.22 GiB for on-demand sampling, while improving runtime only from 5.48 to 4.86 seconds. CCMR at 8K similarly uses 66.68 versus 36.30 GiB. Calling these memory requirements 'similar' obscures a consequential deployment trade-off.

The accuracy claims require qualification. The 332 evaluation pairs come from only three sequences of one synthetic movie, and the supplementary established-dataset evaluations do not test cascaded SEA-RAFT. Moreover, Table 7 reports 1.63 EPE for MS-RAFT+ at quarter resolution, better than cascaded SEA-RAFT's best reported 1.86. The strongest supported accuracy claim concerns fine-detail outliers and large-motion performance on this dataset, rather than general accuracy dominance.

Reproducibility is helped by the pseudocode, rendering script, and software versions, but important benchmarking details remain unspecified, including timing warm-up/synchronization and numerical precision. Because the central contribution is implementation efficiency, these omissions matter more than minor presentation issues.

strengths: The paper makes a useful computational contribution to optical flow: patch-major storage, selective block-sparse correlation computation, and caching exploit spatial and temporal locality while retaining the intended RAFT sampling operator. Compatibility with existing trained models makes this valuable independently of benchmark accuracy improvements.

The high-resolution efficiency gains are substantial and supported by both isolated and end-to-end measurements. Table 3 reduces 8K RAFT inference from 11.00 to 4.59 seconds with nearly unchanged total peak memory, and SEA-RAFT from 2.61 to 1.90 seconds. Table 6 evaluates four GPU architectures and multiple resolutions, feature dimensions, and iteration counts.

The component analysis provides useful supporting evidence: Table 4 quantifies the sparsity benefit of patch-major ordering, while Table 1 measures implementation overheads and demonstrates the benefit of caching.

The 8K evaluation addresses a meaningful gap. The training-free SEA-RAFT cascade substantially improves native-resolution results: large-motion EPE falls from 107.39 to 21.56 and the overall 1-pixel outlier rate from 17.5% to 13.3%. Together with the sampler's demonstrated practical benefits, this supports acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The claimed O(P^1.5) memory bound needs qualification. Section 8.3 requires B to scale as P^(1/8), whereas experiments mostly fix B=8; with fixed B, the dense block mask still occupies O(P^2) space. The derivation also undercounts boundary-crossing lookup blocks, drops a squared factor, and omits the iteration dependence of caching. A corrected bound may retain the stated exponent under fixed-radius, fixed-iteration assumptions, but it does not establish that scaling for the evaluated implementation.

Exact operator equivalence is insufficiently documented. Algorithm 1 marks offsets only through r but gathers through r+1, potentially requiring an unmarked neighboring block for bilinear interpolation. Its block-index expression also contains an extra subtraction of r relative to the subsequent within-block lookup. These may be pseudocode errors, but they obstruct faithful reproduction. The reported unit tests and 0.03% EPE difference are reassuring without resolving boundary handling or establishing numerical equivalence across supported models.

Several efficiency statements overgeneralize the results. At 8K, SEA-RAFT memory increases from 10.25 to 17.21 GiB and CCMR from 36.30 to 66.68 GiB relative to on-demand sampling. At smaller resolutions, dense sampling is frequently faster; Table 6 reports 23 versus 45 ms at width 1024 on GH200. The contribution is a strong high-resolution trade-off, rather than uniformly comparable memory and runtime to both alternatives.

The accuracy claim should be metric-specific. In Table 7, cascaded SEA-RAFT achieves the best overall and large-motion outlier rates, but its best overall EPE of 1.86 is worse than MS-RAFT+'s 1.63. The large native-resolution improvement is convincing, while broad state-of-the-art accuracy language obscures this distinction. The cascade is also a relatively conventional coarse-to-fine initialization, with no ablation of its scale or threshold choices.

The new benchmark contains only three sequences from one synthetic film, limiting evidence for generalization to diverse UHR footage. Although rendering scripts and implementation details help reproducibility, the manuscript does not clearly explain how the four supersampled ground-truth vectors per pixel enter the error metrics, and the custom sampler implementation is not supplied in the reviewed material.
